A multilayer printed circuit board (PCB) designed for optical transmission includes first and second layers with a transparent layer positioned between them. The transparent layer may define a first compartment containing a first mirror configured to receive an incoming light beam.

The first mirror reflects the incoming beam in multiple directions substantially perpendicular to its original direction of travel. In this way, the reflected light distributes an optical signal throughout the first compartment, allowing one or more additional mirrors within the compartment to receive the signal. A second mirror may then redirect the reflected optical signal toward an optical receiver, enabling optical communication through the multilayer PCB.

A multilayer printed circuit board (PCB) is configured to support optical communication between components mounted at different locations on the board. The PCB includes a transparent or optically transmissive layer positioned between two conventional PCB layers. This intermediate layer forms an optical compartment or waveguiding region through which light can travel while the surrounding PCB layers continue to provide electrical interconnections, mechanical support, and protection.

One or more mirrors are arranged within or adjacent to the transparent layer. An incoming light beam, generated by an optical transmitter or introduced through an optical coupling element, strikes a first mirror and is redirected through the optical compartment. Additional mirrors positioned along the propagation path reflect the beam in different, typically perpendicular, directions. In this manner, the optical signal can be routed horizontally and vertically through selected regions of the PCB without requiring a direct line of sight between the transmitter and receiver.

The mirrors may distribute the light to multiple optical paths, allowing the same signal to reach several destinations, or they may guide the beam sequentially toward a particular receiving location. At the destination, a final mirror redirects the light toward an optical receiver, such as a photodiode or another optoelectronic device. The receiver converts the optical signal into an electrical signal for processing by circuitry on the PCB.

By integrating the transparent transmission layer and reflective routing elements into the PCB structure, the design provides an internal optical communication network alongside the board’s conventional electrical connections. This arrangement can reduce dependence on long electrical signal traces, improve signal isolation, and enable high-speed communication among components located across different areas or layers of the PCB.
outputs.L5:
## PCB: The Foundation of Modern Electronics

A printed circuit board (PCB) is the foundation of nearly every modern electronic device. It mechanically supports and electrically connects components such as processors, resistors, capacitors, and sensors through conductive copper pathways.

The PCB manufacturing process begins with a circuit design, which is converted into a physical board layout. Depending on the application, a PCB may have one, two, or multiple conductive layers. Multilayer boards are commonly used in smartphones, computers, vehicles, medical equipment, and industrial systems because they allow complex circuits to fit into compact spaces.

PCB quality directly affects a product’s performance, reliability, and safety. Designers must consider factors such as component placement, signal integrity, heat management, material selection, and manufacturability. Careful testing is also essential to identify defects before the board is installed in the final product.

As electronic devices become smaller and more powerful, PCB technology continues to evolve. Flexible boards, high-density interconnects, and environmentally friendly materials are helping manufacturers meet the demands of the next generation of electronics.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how the beam of light propagates through the transparent compartment of this multilayer PCB and reaches an optical receiver, using patent terminology.
counterfactuals.output:
A light-emitting device launches an optical beam into a light-transmissive compartment formed within the multilayer printed circuit board (PCB). The compartment defines an optical propagation path extending through one or more dielectric layers and may comprise a transparent material, an air-filled cavity, or a waveguide structure bounded by the surrounding PCB layers.

The beam enters the compartment through an optical coupling interface and propagates therein by direct transmission and/or total internal reflection. Optional reflective, refractive, or diffractive features may redirect or confine the beam along the propagation path. At a distal portion of the compartment, an output coupling interface directs the beam onto a photosensitive region of an optical receiver. The optical receiver converts the incident optical radiation into a corresponding electrical signal, which is conveyed through conductive traces or vias of the multilayer PCB.

### Optical Interconnect Printed Circuit Board

An optical interconnect assembly includes a printed circuit board having one or more optical transmission paths integrated within, mounted upon, or positioned adjacent to the printed circuit board. An optical transmitter is configured to emit an optical signal toward a first reflective element. The first reflective element includes a plurality of reflective surfaces, such as angled facets, arranged to redirect respective portions or channels of the optical signal in a plurality of mutually perpendicular directions substantially parallel to a plane of the printed circuit board.

At least one of the redirected optical channels propagates through a waveguide, free-space optical region, or other light-guiding structure to a second reflective element. The second reflective element is oriented to reflect the corresponding optical channel out of the propagation plane and toward an optical receiver. In an embodiment, the second reflective element redirects the optical channel through an angle of approximately ninety degrees toward a photodetector positioned on, above, or below the printed circuit board.

The first reflective element may comprise a pyramidal, polyhedral, faceted, or micro-machined mirror structure having separate reflective facets associated with respective optical channels. For example, a first facet may redirect light along a first in-plane axis, while a second facet redirects light along a second in-plane axis perpendicular to the first in-plane axis. Additional facets may redirect light in opposite directions along either axis, thereby providing multi-directional optical signal distribution from a common transmitter region.

The optical transmission paths may be formed from polymer waveguides, glass waveguides, optical fibers, hollow channels, or free-space cavities. The first and second reflective elements may be metallic mirrors, dielectric mirrors, total-internal-reflection surfaces, or reflective coatings formed directly on the optical transmission paths. Alignment features provided in or on the printed circuit board may position the transmitter, reflective elements, waveguides, and receiver relative to one another.

In operation, light emitted by the transmitter impinges on the first reflective element. The facets of the first reflective element direct individual optical channels in selected perpendicular directions across the printed circuit board. A selected channel reaches the second reflective element, which changes the direction of propagation toward the receiver. The receiver converts the reflected optical signal into an electrical signal for processing by circuitry carried by the printed circuit board.

Such an arrangement enables optical fan-out in multiple orthogonal directions while allowing transmitters and receivers to be mounted using conventional printed-circuit-board assembly techniques. The use of successive reflective elements can reduce optical routing congestion, permit crossing or branching interconnect topologies, and support communication between components located on different surfaces or layers of the printed circuit board.
